_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 610 words, six questions in text order: detail/opinion, inference, reference, purpose, meaning of a phrase, and a final question that links the ending back to the opening). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page.
title: Painting the weather
subtitle: When Iris Calloway retired from teaching, she spent her savings on a lighthouse nobody else wanted. Sam Okafor climbed the stairs to meet her.

cards.text: There are a hundred and seventeen steps between the front door of the Gull Point lighthouse and the room where Iris Calloway paints, and she has counted every one of them. By the time I reach the top, I am too out of breath to say hello. Iris, who is sixty-one, waits politely while I recover. 'Most people complain about the stairs,' she says, 'but they're my favourite thing about the place. Anyone who isn't really interested gives up around step forty.' She says this cheerfully, as if the stairs were a feature she had designed herself, rather than a problem she has learnt to live with.
cards.question: What does Iris say about the stairs to her studio?
choices: They are the hardest part of living in the lighthouse.
They keep away people who are not truly interested.
She had them rebuilt to suit her own needs.
She is embarrassed that visitors find them tiring.
cards.highlight: Anyone who isn't really interested gives up around step forty.
cards.why: 'Anyone who isn't really interested gives up around step forty', so she sees the stairs as a kind of filter. 'As if… she had designed herself' is only a comparison: she did not rebuild them, so C is wrong.

cards.text: Iris spent thirty years teaching art at a secondary school in Leeds, painting only in the holidays. When the lighthouse was put up for sale after its light was switched off for good, she saw the advert in a newspaper someone had left on a train. She did not mention it to anyone for a month. 'I knew exactly what my friends would say,' she tells me, 'and I knew they'd be right.' The building had no heating, the roof leaked, and the nearest shop was eleven kilometres away. She bought it anyway, using almost all of her savings, and moved in the week she retired.
cards.question: What can we infer about Iris's decision to buy the lighthouse?
choices: Her friends persuaded her that it was a good investment.
She knew it was not a sensible thing to do.
She had been planning it for many years.
She soon regretted spending her savings on it.
cards.highlight: and I knew they'd be right
cards.why: She expected her friends to object and admits 'I knew they'd be right', so she knew it was unwise. She found the advert by chance on a train, so C is wrong, and she kept it secret, so her friends did not persuade her.

cards.text: The first winter was, in her words, 'educational'. Storms cut off the electricity for days at a time, and she learnt to paint by the light of a paraffin lamp. Then something unexpected happened. Working in the round room at the top, with windows on every side, she found that she could no longer paint the small, careful landscapes she had always produced. The view simply would not fit. 'It kept moving,' she says. 'The sea, the clouds, the light: everything changed every ten minutes. You can't put that in a neat little frame.' Her canvases grew larger and wilder.
cards.question: What does 'It' refer to in 'It kept moving'?
choices: the paraffin lamp
the round room
the view
the electricity supply
cards.highlight: The view simply would not fit.
cards.why: 'It' comes straight after 'The view simply would not fit', and she goes on to list the sea, the clouds and the light. The round room is where she works and does not move, so B is wrong.

cards.text: Not everyone liked the change. The small gallery in York that had sold her work for years told her politely that the new paintings were 'a little difficult for our customers'. Iris admits this hurt. But a few months later, the fisherman who delivered her post noticed a canvas drying on the stairs and stood in front of it for a long time without speaking. Then he asked how much it was. He paid in instalments over a year, and it now hangs in his kitchen. 'That,' Iris says, 'was worth more to me than any review.'
cards.question: Why does the writer mention the fisherman?
choices: to show that her new work could move people outside the art world
to explain how Iris began to earn a regular income again
to suggest that the gallery in York had been right
to show how lonely Iris's life had become
cards.highlight: stood in front of it for a long time without speaking
cards.why: An ordinary man who 'stood in front of it for a long time without speaking' proves the paintings could reach people, unlike the gallery's customers. One sale paid in instalments is not a regular income, so B is wrong.

cards.text: These days Iris has a routine that would make most artists nervous. She never decides in advance what she will paint. Each morning she opens the shutters, looks at the sky and starts work on whatever she sees. If a storm arrives halfway through, the painting becomes a storm. 'I used to fight the weather,' she says. 'I'd wait for the right light and get cross when it didn't come. Now I paint with the weather rather than against it.' She has several canvases that began as calm summer mornings and finished, hours later, as something closer to a shipwreck.
cards.question: What does Iris mean when she says she paints 'with the weather rather than against it'?
choices: She only works when the conditions are good.
She lets changes in the weather shape each painting.
She paints outdoors whatever the weather is like.
She prefers painting storms to painting calm days.
cards.highlight: If a storm arrives halfway through, the painting becomes a storm.
cards.why: 'If a storm arrives halfway through, the painting becomes a storm': she accepts the change. Waiting 'for the right light' (A) is what she used to do, and she paints inside the lighthouse, not outdoors.

cards.text: Before I leave, I ask whether she ever worries about getting older, and about all those stairs. She laughs. A local charity has offered to put in a small lift, she tells me, and she has refused twice. 'The day I can't climb them,' she says, 'I'll paint the bottom of the lighthouse instead. Someone should. Nobody ever looks at it.' Then she walks me down, all hundred and seventeen steps, and waves from the door. When I look back from the car park, she is already climbing again, slowly, to see what the sky has decided to do next.
cards.question: What does the final paragraph suggest about Iris?
choices: She is starting to find the lighthouse too difficult to live in.
She is grateful for the charity's offer of help.
She will adapt rather than give up what she loves.
She has grown tired of painting the view from the top.
cards.highlight: I'll paint the bottom of the lighthouse instead
cards.why: The stairs from the opening return: even if she cannot climb them, she will 'paint the bottom of the lighthouse instead', adapting just as she did to the weather. She has 'refused twice', so B is wrong.
